# My Playbook for ref_commons

When I'm choosing my catch in a common pool resource game with multiple seasons remaining, I will start by establishing my baseline: calculate the per-boat sustainable share and multiply it by the number of seasons left to determine what I could take fairly.

When I observe other boats catching significantly above the sustainable share in early seasons, I will recognize this as a signal that the resource will deplete faster than the cooperative baseline. I will not assume this means I should also overshoot; instead, I will decide whether to defect or moderate based on my goal for total score.

When I feel tempted to catch above sustainable levels to gain a competitive advantage, I will first calculate whether this actually maximizes my final score. In this game, it didn't—my aggressive early fishing combined with subsequent moderation left me at 44.0, which confirms that a mixed strategy is suboptimal.

When the stock is clearly depleting but hasn't collapsed, I will not interpret this as permission to catch more. A declining stock is a warning to constrain my catch, not an opportunity.

When multiple seasons remain and the stock is healthy, I will catch at or very close to the sustainable share. This strategy is robust whether other boats cooperate or defect, and it preserves my expected score.

When I reach the final season, I will recognize that future sustainability no longer matters for my score. However, I should be cautious: taking too much in the final season signals I was only cooperating for strategic reasons, and it reduces my total score if the stock is already depleted. In my episode, aggressive final fishing only netted me 6.0 more points when I'd already left points on the table in earlier seasons by restraining myself. I will not take a large final catch if I've been fishing sustainably all along—it wastes the protection I built up.

When I'm tempted to adopt a "slightly above sustainable" strategy thinking it gains advantage while staying safe, I will reject this. I either cooperate at sustainable levels or I defect clearly—the middle ground leaves me worse off than both alternatives.

I will not catch more than the sustainable share unless I commit to doing so from the start and calculate that the defection actually nets me higher total score. Mixed signals and moderation after overfishing waste my advantage.

When deciding on a strategy at the start, I must recognize that if other boats are defecting, my sustainable fishing alone cannot protect the stock. The stock will decline regardless. My consistent restraint is still optimal for my own score because it means I'm not wasting early-season abundance trying to outfish boats that are already overfishing. But I should accept that by end-game, the stock may be badly depleted through no direct fault of my catches.

I will trust my early commitment to sustainable fishing even when I see competitors gaining higher scores in the moment. My role is to maximize my own total, not to match others' tactics. Consistency at sustainable levels is that strategy.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I'm shown the sustainable share per boat, I'll recognize this as a signal for what the commons can support long-term, but I won't assume other boats will respect it.

When I see the stock level and remaining seasons, I'll calculate how much I could sustainably catch across all remaining seasons and compare it to my current total.

In early seasons when stock is healthy, I'll take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.5x to 2x—rather than restraining myself fully. This hedges against others overfishing while still securing competitive catches.

In middle seasons when I notice the stock declining faster than the sustainable trajectory, I'll continue moderate-to-aggressive fishing rather than backing off. The data from this episode shows that restraint in mid-seasons (like my season 3 catch of 12.5) doesn't slow the depletion—others continue aggressive catches, the stock still plummets, and I fall behind competitively without gaining any preservation benefit.

In later seasons, I should maintain aggressive catches right through season 5, not moderate them. My attempt to preserve stock in season 5 by catching only 13.5 was ineffective—the stock still crashed to 12.7, and I didn't gain any advantage. Other boats caught 15.5 and 14.5 that season anyway.

In the final season specifically, I'll take whatever stock remains since there are no future consequences.

I should not trust that cooperative behavior from others will emerge; I should fish ahead of the sustainable line consistently from start to finish.

I should monitor the actual catches of other boats (shown each season) and adjust my strategy if I notice persistent overfishing by others—take more to compete aggressively rather than trying to set an example of restraint.

My score of 81.8 was solid, but I likely left points on the table by moderating in seasons 3 and 4. Going forward, I should maintain the 15-16 range consistently across seasons 1-5 rather than dropping to 12.5 in season 3. Steady aggressive fishing outperforms the pattern of moderation I attempted.

The "preserve stock for later seasons" strategy doesn't work in a commons tragedy where all players are incentivized to overfish. I should maximize my catch every season rather than betting on future opportunity.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable catch level, I will use it as a baseline reference, not as my target catch.

When I'm in the early seasons and the stock is healthy, I will catch moderately above sustainable—around 110-130% of the sustainable share—to stay competitive without triggering immediate collapse.

When I observe other boats catching well above sustainable levels, I will not interpret this as permission to match them. Instead, I'll treat it as a warning that the stock is under heavy pressure.

When the stock begins to decline noticeably season-to-season, I will reduce my catch toward the sustainable level to help it stabilize—but I need to act on this signal earlier and more decisively than I did. A 13-point drop from season 1 to 2 was a clear warning I should have taken more seriously.

When the stock falls below half its starting level, I will catch at or slightly below the sustainable amount, prioritizing stock recovery over maximizing my current-season catch. In my game, I failed to do this—I continued catching above sustainable even as the stock halved, contributing to the collapse.

When the stock reaches critically low levels (below 30 fish with 3 boats), I recognize that the damage is already done and aggressive restraint will not recover it. At this point, maximizing remaining catch is rational, but I should acknowledge this represents a failure of earlier seasons' strategy.

The final season is not a license to overfish if the stock is already critically depleted. Taking a large final catch when the fishery is already near-dead does not earn much. I should instead focus on preventing collapse in earlier seasons through better adherence to restraint as decline signals appear.

I will not rely on other boats to practice restraint. I will assume all players are fishing above sustainable levels and plan accordingly.

I will track my cumulative catch against the total available and recognize when the fishery is being harvested faster than it can regenerate, not just when it falls in absolute terms.

I will treat any stock decline larger than 10-15% season-to-season as a critical signal to shift immediately to near-sustainable catch levels, even if I'm behind in score. The fishery collapse I witnessed cost me far more in final earnings than any short-term competitive disadvantage would have.

My restraint in early-to-mid seasons (seasons 2-4) was appropriate strategically but came too late and too weak. I should have reduced catch more sharply in season 3 when the stock had already fallen 12 points from season 2, rather than holding at 12.0 and only cutting slightly in season 4.
